At the bus stand in their small town, Vidya told anyone who would listen that Jasleen had simply changed. "She found new friends in the other section and dropped me. Totally fake." Her cousin nodded along on the ride home.
Vidya left out Jasleen's birthday, when she had laughed with the others at Jasleen's homemade cake, and the message Jasleen sent afterwards, which Vidya never answered. Whenever that memory came up, she pushed it away and went back to the easier version.
A month later, at the temple fair, Vidya snapped at a new girl from her class for being late and walked off. Standing alone by the bangle stalls, she felt a flicker of the same heavy feeling. She didn't let herself look at it.

qa.q: What did Vidya say Jasleen had done?
qa.a: Vidya said Jasleen found new friends in the other section and dropped her.

qa.q: Why does Vidya keep going back to the easier version?
qa.a: It eases her guilt about laughing at Jasleen's homemade cake and ignoring her message, so she avoids the memory.

qa.q: What could Vidya do when that heavy feeling comes back?
qa.a: She could let herself look at the birthday memory honestly, perhaps talk it through with someone she trusts, and think about answering Jasleen.

qa.q: How might Jasleen tell the story of the lost friendship?
qa.a: Jasleen would probably remember being laughed at on her birthday and an unanswered message, not simply changing and dropping Vidya.

grounding: A teenage girl blames a lost friend entirely, and the flattering story eases her guilt while blocking the learning she needs for the next friendship.

In Oslo the snow had turned grey, and Astrid stamped it off her boots in the hallway. "Mei sat with the new girl again," she told her mother. "She's so two-faced. I did nothing."
Her mother looked up from the soup. "Nothing at all? Didn't you two argue after the concert?"
"That was ages ago. And she was being dramatic."
Astrid didn't mention that she had told the choir girls Mei's secret about her parents' divorce, the one Mei had begged her to keep. She had almost forgotten it herself, or rather had stopped letting herself remember.
"Maybe ask her what happened from her side?" her mother said.
"Why should I? She's the problem." Astrid went to her room and shut the door, and the version where she did nothing felt safe again.

qa.q: What did Astrid tell the choir girls?
qa.a: Astrid told them Mei's secret about her parents' divorce, the one Mei had begged her to keep.

qa.q: Why does Astrid insist she did nothing?
qa.a: Remembering that she spilled Mei's secret would bring guilt, so the story where Mei is the problem feels safer.

qa.q: What would help Astrid learn from this before her next friendship?
qa.a: She could take her mother's suggestion, ask Mei about her side, and own up to sharing the secret, which could begin a repair.

qa.q: What is it like for Mei after her secret was shared?
qa.a: Mei probably feels betrayed and exposed, so keeping away from Astrid may be her way of protecting herself.

grounding: A teenage girl insists Mei is the only problem, and the flattering story keeps her from facing the guilt that could teach her something.

passage:
I'm Jasleen, and last term I lost my best friend, Sahil. For months I told everyone the same story: Sahil changed. He got new friends in the cricket team. He stopped replying. He got arrogant.
It felt good to say. Each time, people nodded, and I felt a little lighter.
Then, last week, clearing my phone, I found our old chat. His messages were there: "coming for the movie?" "you ok?" "missed you at the bus stop." And under them, mine: "busy," "maybe," "next time." Again and again.
I closed the chat fast. My face felt hot. I told myself he could have tried harder.
But I keep thinking about it. If my story is true, why were there so many of his messages and so few of mine? I'm not ready to say it's my fault. But I think my story left some parts out.

qa.q: What were some of Sahil's messages in the old chat?
qa.a: His messages were "coming for the movie?", "you ok?" and "missed you at the bus stop."

qa.q: Why did Jasleen close the chat so fast?
qa.a: Jasleen felt ashamed and uncomfortable, because the messages challenged the comforting story that Sahil was the only one to blame.

qa.q: What small step could help Jasleen learn from this?
qa.a: Jasleen could reread the chat honestly, name one thing she did, and maybe send Sahil a short message to reconnect.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt during those months of "busy" and "maybe"?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt ignored and hurt, which could explain why he spent more time with the cricket team.

grounding: It shows a teenager blaming a lost friendship entirely on the other person, a story that eases guilt but blocks learning until evidence cracks it.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Wednesday, Class 10.
Zeenat came to see me about "a toxic friend." She spoke for twenty minutes about Parveen: Parveen was jealous, Parveen was two-faced, Parveen turned the class against her. When I asked how the fight started, Zeenat said, "It doesn't matter. She's just like that."
Later she mentioned, very quickly, that she had told a few girls about Parveen's parents' divorce, "but only because everyone would find out anyway." Then she went straight back to Parveen's faults.
Zeenat's jaw was tight and she wouldn't look at me during that part. I think she knows, somewhere, but the other story is easier to carry.
I didn't argue. I asked, "If a friend of yours told you this story, which part would you want to hear more about?" She was quiet a long time. We will meet again on Monday. I have asked her to write down one thing she might do differently next time.

qa.q: What did Zeenat tell a few girls about?
qa.a: She told a few girls about Parveen's parents' divorce.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's tight jaw suggest when she mentions the divorce?
qa.a: It suggests Zeenat feels guilty and uncomfortable about her own part, even while insisting Parveen is the whole problem.

qa.q: How did the counsellor support Zeenat without attacking her?
qa.a: The counsellor didn't argue but asked a gentle question about which part a friend would want to hear more about, and set a small writing task.

qa.q: How might Parveen have experienced the fight?
qa.a: Parveen likely felt betrayed and exposed, since something private about her family was shared with other girls.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teenager insisting a lost friend was the only problem, a story that eases guilt but blocks learning.

passage:
Friday night
Pallavi walked past me at the canteen today like I was invisible. Fine. I don't care. She's the one who ruined everything.
Things Pallavi did: 1. Sat with the new girls on sports day. 2. Didn't laugh at my joke about her singing. 3. Told Ma'am I copied her project idea (I didn't copy, I just had the same idea).
Things I did: …nothing really. Okay, I laughed at her singing in front of the whole class. But it was a joke. She's too sensitive. Everyone says so.
Mummy asked why Pallavi hasn't come over. I said, "She's changed." Mummy said, "People don't usually change for no reason, Irawati." I went to my room.
I'm not writing more. It was her fault. Mostly.
Probably.

qa.q: What did Irawati laugh at in front of the whole class?
qa.a: Irawati laughed at Pallavi's singing in front of the whole class.

qa.q: How does Irawati feel as the diary entry ends with "Mostly. Probably."?
qa.a: Irawati feels defensive and uneasy, beginning to doubt the story that Pallavi was completely to blame.

qa.q: What could Irawati try instead of listing only Pallavi's faults?
qa.a: Irawati could finish the "Things I did" list honestly and think about apologising for the joke, which might help this or her next friendship.

qa.q: How might Pallavi see what happened?
qa.a: Pallavi probably felt humiliated by the joke about her singing and hurt, which might explain why she sat with the new girls.

grounding: A teenager's diary builds a flattering story blaming a lost friend, easing guilt while blocking the learning that could repair things.
